meta.title: Lelia — buy less, wear what you own
meta.description: Check a piece while you’re still in the shop: how many outfits it makes with your wardrobe, whether you already own something like it, and what each wear will cost. No account, nothing uploaded. Free for iPhone.
hero.title: Buy less. Wear what you own.
hero.lede: Photograph a piece in the shop and Lelia asks your wardrobe: how many new outfits it makes, whether you already own something like it, and what one outing in it will cost. Then you decide.
hero.alt: Lelia’s check before buying: one word for the verdict, how many new outfits the piece makes with your wardrobe, and the pieces you already own.
trust.upload.dt: Your things stay on the phone
trust.upload.dd: Photos and wardrobe are never sent anywhere.
trust.account.dd: No email, no password, no profile on a server.
trust.model.dd: Colour is measured, not guessed — and every score shows its working.
own.h: Lay it down. The app does the rest.
own.alt: Adding several photos in Lelia: “Import: 19 photos”, a line saying there are no duplicates, a “Remove background” switch and the list of pieces — each with a suggested type and colour you can change — and an “Add 19 pieces” button.
wedge.h: Every other app hands you a number. Lelia tells you what it is made of.
wedge.score.note: A score, and no way to find out where it came from.
quote.reason1: “Neutral, and its faint warmth matches yours — a colour like this always works”
quote.reason2: “The colour is warmer than your skin’s undertone — of the three axes, temperature is what costs the most points here”
wedge.p: Every score is tappable, and every tap explains that particular piece: what is off about it and where it is better worn.
wedge.alt: Lelia’s “How the scores work” screen: the two scores — how pieces go together and how a colour suits your looks — what each is made of, and a scale of what the numbers mean.
outfits.alt: Lelia’s home: the day panel with the weather and an outfit built around a piece you haven’t worn in a while, and all your outfits below.
builder.alt: Lelia’s outfit builder: a figure made of the chosen pieces, a score, and rows of candidates for top, bottom, shoes, outerwear and accessories, with the chosen ones outlined.
calendar.h: What in your closet works — and what just hangs there?
calendar.lede: Log what you wore, or plan an outfit ahead. Lelia builds home-screen outfits from the pieces that have waited longest.
calendar.stats.h: How much of your wardrobe is in use
calendar.alt: Lelia’s wear log: a month with worn days marked, the selected day with its pieces and the “Add what you wore” and “Plan an outfit” buttons.
shop.h: Should you buy it? Ask your wardrobe — before the till.
shop.lede: Snap the piece, answer three questions — and Lelia weighs it against what already hangs in your wardrobe.
verdict.alt: A verdict in Lelia: the piece’s photo, one word and the main line, the price field, how many outfits it adds and whether you own something similar, with “Decide later” and “Buying” at the bottom.
faq.cost.a: Right now, nothing: no ads, no account and no payments. Later we plan an optional Plus subscription for extra depth. Everyone who installs Lelia before Plus launches gets Plus free, for good. When it arrives, this page and the app will say plainly what stays free for everyone else.
faq.color.q: What if the photo lies about the colour?
faq.color.a: Then you tell it otherwise. Tap the item with the eyedropper, or pick the shade from the palette — and your answer sticks instead of being recalculated away. For pale neutrals the app asks first rather than guessing, because a warm bulb turns white into cream and grey into beige.
faq.move.q: Can I move my wardrobe to a new phone?
faq.move.a: Yes — as a file. In Settings, save a wardrobe backup: items with their photos, outfits, plans, the wear log, trips and the wishlist go into one archive, wherever you send it. On the new phone, restore from it. There is still no cloud and no sync — the backup is yours to make.
faq.suits.q: Why is “suits you” separate from the outfit score?
faq.suits.a: Because they answer different questions. Harmony is how pieces relate to each other; “suits you” is how a colour relates to your face. Blend them and neither can be explained.
faq.where.a: On the App Store, free, for iPhone. There is nothing to sign up for: the app asks for your language, then offers a sample wardrobe and a sample piece to check — so you can see the verdict in a minute, before photographing anything of your own.
finale.lede: Lelia is for making them usable again — quietly, on one phone, with its reasoning in the open.
finale.fineprint: Free to download  ·  no account  ·  no ads
footer.cookies: This page sets no tracking cookies
footer.note: An independent project, not affiliated with any other company, brand, or application using the name Lelia.
privacy.meta.title: Privacy policy — Lelia
privacy.meta.description: Lelia keeps nothing that identifies you. Your wardrobe, your photos and your colour profile stay on your iPhone. This page says exactly what leaves it and what does not.
privacy.lede: Lelia is a wardrobe app that runs on your iPhone. There are no accounts and no servers holding your things. Three things do leave the phone, and this page names all three.
privacy.collect.p1: Nothing that identifies you. We do not collect, transmit, sell or share your name, your contacts, your photos, your wardrobe or your location. The app does send anonymous usage counts and crash reports, with a few technical details about the device, which you can switch off — Usage statistics below says exactly what they are.
privacy.collect.p2: There is no sign-up and no login, so we have no way of knowing who you are. The usage counts carry only a random identifier created when the app is installed; it is not linked to a person or an account, and we have nothing to link it with.
privacy.device.h: What the app keeps on your device
privacy.device.p: Everything you put into Lelia stays in the app’s own storage on your iPhone:
privacy.device.li1: photos of your clothes, including the ones taken with the camera inside the app, and — if you remove the background — the cut-out next to the original;
privacy.device.li2: your wardrobe: categories, colours, patterns and the outfits you build;
privacy.device.li3: a record of what you wore and when;
privacy.device.li4: your colour-type profile: the hair, eye and skin colours you pick — by hand or from a photo of yourself — your answers to the three questions, and the resulting type. The photo is used only while you pick colours from it; it is not saved to your wardrobe or your profile;
privacy.device.li7: your trips: the destination, the dates, the forecast for each day and the packing list with its ticks;
privacy.device.li8: your wishlist: photos and notes about things you are thinking of buying, and the app’s verdict on them;
privacy.device.li9: outfits planned for upcoming days, and the occasion you named for them;
privacy.device.after: None of this leaves your device unless you save a backup yourself (see below). We cannot see it and we cannot recover it. Deleting the app deletes all of it for good — Lelia does not sync and keeps no copy in the cloud.
privacy.permissions.li1: Camera — to photograph your clothes and, if you choose, to take a selfie to find your colour type. Photos are processed on the device. Clothing photos are saved into the app’s own storage; the selfie is not.
privacy.permissions.li2: Photo library (read) — to add clothes, or a photo of yourself for the colour type, from photos you already have. Lelia reads only the photos you pick yourself.
privacy.permissions.li3: Photo library (add) — to save a photo of an item, or a picture of an outfit, to your library when you ask it to.
privacy.permissions.li4: Location (while using the app) — only if you turn on weather, and only to look up today’s forecast. You can name a city instead and never grant it.
privacy.permissions.li5: Notifications — only if you turn them on. They are local: the phone itself schedules them, with no server and no push token, so nothing but your iPhone knows what to remind you of and when. Silent, at most one a morning; switch them off in Wardrobe → ⚙ Settings → Notifications.
privacy.permissions.after: Any of these can be revoked in iOS settings; the rest of the app keeps working.
privacy.vision.p: On iOS 17 and later, Lelia uses Apple’s Vision framework to cut a piece out of its background and to suggest its type — a shirt, trousers, boots. This runs entirely on your iPhone: no photo and no result is sent to us, to Apple or to anyone else. The suggestion is only a starting point, and you can change it. Colours, scores and outfits are worked out by the app’s own formulas, not by a model.
privacy.network.p1: Lelia makes three kinds of network request, and no others. On launch it asks Expo’s update service (u.expo.dev) whether a newer version of the app’s JavaScript is available. That request carries the platform, the app’s runtime version and the update channel; as with any request over the internet, the service also sees your IP address. It carries nothing from your wardrobe: no photos, no items, no profile.
privacy.network.p2: The service is run by Expo, Inc. under its own policy: expo.dev/privacy.
privacy.network.p3: The other two are described below: anonymous usage statistics with crash reports, and the weather. There is no advertising and no third-party tracking SDK. The app never asks for permission to track you across other apps or websites, because it does not. When you share an outfit or a trip, or save a backup, the file goes to the iOS share sheet and from there only where you send it; Lelia itself uploads nothing.
privacy.analytics.p1: Lelia counts how the app is used, through PostHog. The events are anonymous: when the app is opened and which screens are opened, including each step of the introduction and which way you chose to start; when adding a piece was started, and when a piece is added or removed, with its category only; how long it took from the first launch to the first piece and the first outfit, in seconds; whether the demo wardrobe was added or removed; whether a suggested type or colour was kept or changed by hand, and whether removing the background worked; whether the colour-type questions were finished and a score’s explanation was opened; whether an outfit was opened, saved, worn, planned ahead or shared — for a plan, only how many days ahead and whether an occasion was named, never the name itself; whether a shop check showed a verdict and which decision was made — the verdict band, the number of outfits and similar pieces, and whether a price was entered, never the price or the photo; which challenges were started and finished and whether their cards were shared; how trips, the weather suggestions, the wishlist and importing several photos are used; whether a backup was saved or restored, with the number of items only; and whether notifications were turned on. The events themselves are numbers and short labels.
privacy.analytics.tech: Alongside each event, PostHog receives the standard technical details its library adds: that random install identifier and a session identifier, the device model, the iOS and app versions, the screen size, the language and region setting, and the time zone. Your connection’s IP address reaches PostHog as with any request over the internet; the project is set to discard it rather than store it.
privacy.analytics.crash: Crash reports. If the app hits an error it did not expect, or closes because of one, it sends a report to the same PostHog project: the type and text of the error, where in the app’s code it happened, and the same technical details as the events. Reports carry nothing from your wardrobe, and the app does not send what it writes to its own log.
privacy.analytics.p2: What is never sent: your photos or their file paths, your notes, brands or item names, the colours of your clothes, your name, your location and where you travel. PostHog is also told not to work out a country or city from your connection. No profile is created for you, and screen recording is switched off. PostHog stores the events in the European Union and acts as a processor on our behalf; its own policy is at posthog.com/privacy.
privacy.analytics.p3: Counting starts on the first launch, so we can see where people get stuck before their first piece and first outfit. You can switch it off at any time in Wardrobe → ⚙ Settings → Data → Anonymous usage statistics; that stops both the statistics and the crash reports, and the choice survives “Reset everything”.
privacy.weather.p1: The Home tab can show the weather and pick outfits for it. This is off until you turn it on, and the app works fully without it.
privacy.weather.p2: To look up the forecast it needs a place — either this device’s location, or a city you type in; the name you type is sent to Open-Meteo’s place search to find it. Coordinates are rounded to about 11 kilometres before they are sent, so a request says roughly which town you are in and nothing closer. Trips use the same service: to plan one, the app sends the destination’s rounded coordinates and the trip dates. If notifications about sharp weather changes are on, the app asks the same service for today’s and tomorrow’s forecast for the same rounded place when you open it. All of this goes to Open-Meteo and nowhere else, carries nothing from your wardrobe, and is not stored by us. Turning weather off erases the saved place; resetting your profile erases it together with your trips.
privacy.backup.p1: In Settings you can save a wardrobe backup as a single file (.zip): item photos, items, outfits and plans, the wear log, trips, the wishlist and your colour type. The file is put together on the phone and handed to the iOS share sheet — to wherever you send it yourself: Files, AirDrop, email or a cloud drive. We never receive it or see it.
privacy.backup.p2: The file is not encrypted, so keep it the way you would keep the photos themselves. Restoring from a backup replaces everything currently in the app; the statistics and notification settings stay as they are on this phone.
privacy.children.p: Lelia collects nothing that identifies anyone, children included.
privacy.site.p: The site counts visits through the same PostHog project (in the EU): which pages are opened, where visitors came from (the referring site or a link tag), how far down they scroll, which language they pick, and whether they tap the App Store button. There are no cookies and nothing is stored in your browser — each page load is a separate anonymous visit, and we cannot tell when you come back. No city or country is worked out from your IP, and there is no screen recording. If your browser sends “Do Not Track”, the page counts nothing at all. The link to the App Store carries a campaign tag — where you came from and which button you tapped — so App Store Connect can show which links bring people in; it says nothing about you.
privacy.rights.p: We hold nothing that identifies you. Your wardrobe is on your device and under your control: delete individual items inside the app, use “Reset everything” in Settings, or delete the app to remove everything at once. Backups you saved are wherever you put them, and are deleted there. The usage counts and crash reports carry only a random identifier we cannot connect to you, so we cannot find yours to hand over or delete; switching statistics off in Settings stops them.
privacy.changes.p: If this policy changes, the new version appears at this same address with a new date, and anything substantive is named in the app’s release notes.
privacy.contact.p: Questions about this policy, or about the app:
today.h: Every morning, an outfit from what’s been waiting.
today.lede: The top of Home is outfits built from pieces you haven’t worn in a while. Tap “I’ll wear this” and the day is logged.
today.picks.h: The picks grow on their own
today.picks.p: Add a piece and the suggestions top themselves up.
today.build.p: Slot by slot — the score changes with every swap.
trips.h: The smallest suitcase for every day away.
trips.lede: Give it a city and dates — Lelia checks the forecast for each day and builds the shortest packing list that covers the whole trip.
trips.alt: Packing in Lelia: a suitcase picture that fills with every tick, the weather for each day of the trip, and the packing list by category.
own.first.p: Pick a dozen photos at once — or start with the sample and see a check in a minute.
faq.offline.a: Yes. The wardrobe, outfits, explanations, planning and checking an item all work in airplane mode. The network is only needed for the weather and a trip’s forecast.
faq.data.a: Your clothes, photos, outfits and colour type live only on your phone — we never see them. The app sends anonymous usage statistics and crash reports with no photos or item names, and you can switch them off in Settings. The privacy policy has the details.
cost.h: The cheaper jacket can cost you more.
cost.lede: The price tag ÷ how many times you’ll actually wear it.
cost.note: Every piece in Lelia shows its own cost per wear. The ones sitting idle ask for a decision: wear, set aside or give away.
challenges.lede: A challenge turns “buy less” into a game with an end and a result.
challenges.ten.p: Ten pieces, ten days — a new outfit from only them every day.
challenges.capsule.p: 33 pieces, shoes and accessories included, for three months. The rest of the wardrobe takes a break.
challenges.nobuy.p: Thirty days of nothing new — every “Not buying” goes into “saved”.
challenges.friends: Invite a friend with a link: you start the same challenge on the same day and compare cards in your chat. No accounts, no server.
challenge.meta.title: A challenge for two — Lelia
challenge.meta.description: A friend invited you to a Lelia challenge: wear what you own, buy less, compare progress.
challenge.lede: Games with an end and a result: wear what you own, buy less, compare progress with a friend.
challenge.how.li1: Install Lelia and add your clothes — or start with the sample wardrobe.
challenge.how.li2: Open this link on your iPhone and tap “Open in Lelia”: the same challenge and start day are filled in.
challenge.how.li3: Share progress cards with each other in your chat. Everything is counted on your own phone.
challenge.fine: No account and no server: your wardrobe and progress never leave your phone.
challenge.rule.ten_ten: 10 pieces, 10 days — an outfit from just these every day.
challenge.rule.capsule: 33 pieces including shoes and accessories for three months — the rest takes a break.
challenge.rule.no_buy: 30 days with nothing new. Checking pieces in shops is fine — buying isn’t.
challenge.rule.budget: You set the limit — and see how much is left.
challenge.rule.forgotten: Within two weeks, wear 5 pieces that haven’t been worn for 60+ days.
challenge.rule.second_life: One to three months of buying only second-hand, vintage or swaps.
not.shop.h: Not a shop, not a shopping feed
not.shop.p: No catalogue, no “new arrivals”, no “you might also like”. The app starts with what already hangs in your wardrobe, not with what you could add to it.
not.ads.p: No banners, no “similar items”, no commission from shops. Lelia earns nothing from what you buy — which is why it can honestly say “you already have this”.
not.feed.p: No followers, no likes, no feed of other people’s new buys. The only thing you can share is a challenge card — how many times you wore what you already owned.
not.coda: No account, no cloud: your clothes and photos stay on your phone.
faq.anyway.q: What if I still want to buy it?
faq.anyway.a: Then buy it — it’s your call. Lelia doesn’t forbid anything; it shows what similar pieces you already own and how many of your clothes the new one goes with. Unsure? Add it to your wishlist and decide later. Buying? It goes straight into your wardrobe and starts counting cost per wear.
faq.saved.a: Simply: when you tap “Not buying” after a check and you entered a price, that amount goes into “saved”. Pieces without a price and pieces on your wishlist don’t count — no projections, no “could have spent”.
faq.cant.a: It doesn’t recognise fabric, pattern or brand — Vision only suggests the type of piece, and you pick the fabric and pattern. And it doesn’t judge cut, fit or size: the app looks at colour, pattern, occasion and season; whether a piece suits your body is up to you.
faq.device.q: Is there an Android or iPad version?
faq.device.a: Not yet — iPhone only. There’s no sync between devices either: your wardrobe lives on one phone and moves to a new one as a file.
flow.aria: How a decision in the shop goes
flow.s1.p: Right on the hanger — the app removes the background itself.
flow.s2.p: Does the colour look right? What is it? Plain or patterned?
flow.s3.p: Take it, think it over or walk past — and why:
flow.buy.p: The piece goes straight into your wardrobe and starts counting its cost per wear.
flow.later.p: The piece waits in the Check tab. Three days later the app asks whether you still want it.
flow.save.p: Its price goes into “saved” — your Diary shows how much stayed in your pocket.
cost.chart.aria: Chart: the trendy jacket’s cost per wear stops at €15 after 4 wears; the €150 simple jacket gets cheaper with every wear, matches the trendy one at wear 10 and reaches €2.50 by wear 60.
cost.chart.simple: Simple, €150: 60 wears over a few seasons.
cost.chart.cross: At wear 10 the pricier jacket becomes the better deal
dots.aria: Example wardrobe of 40 pieces: 8 worn often, 5 once or twice, 27 not worn for three months.
dots.caption: Example: of 40 pieces, 13 were worn in three months — a third of the wardrobe is in use.
weights.title: What a pair’s score is made of
weights.note: No model that “just decided”. The parts are multiplied, so one failed part pulls the whole score down: even a perfect colour can’t rescue a puffer with linen shorts.
trips.viz.bag: 5 days — 8 pieces in the suitcase. Each one works in several outfits.
trips.viz.aria: Example five-day trip: weather and an outfit for each day, and just eight pieces in the suitcase, repeated across days.
challenges.more.label: And three more:
own.s1.h: Lay the piece on a plain surface and snap it
own.s1.p: Just make sure the background isn’t the same colour.
own.s2.p: Apple’s on-device Vision does it and suggests the type — you can change it.
own.s3.p: And if it can’t see the edge, it doesn’t guess — you get a dropper and a palette.
